fact: Randy Levine was sentenced to four years in prison on a Friday, after being on the run for almost 15 years, according to Justice Department officials.
Levine is 54 years old and is from Boca Raton, Florida.
Austrian authorities were able to identify Randy Levine due to a facial recognition system, according to the DOJ.
Levine tried to use an alias to open a bank account in Austria, which led to his arrest in June 2020.
According to Levine's plea agreement, which he signed in May, he would offer to set up gambling accounts for people if they sent him money.
Levine reportedly played a recording of casino sounds while he was on calls with victims.
Levine made calls to victims using a Las Vegas phone number.
Levine came under investigation by the FBI.
Levine was able to get a replacement for the passport that law enforcement officials seized by claiming the passport had simply been lost.
Levine eventually ended up in Poland, where he was arrested in 2008.
There was a legal battle over whether Levine could be extradited to the US, which continued until late 2011.
By the time Polish courts had decided that Levine could be extradited, Levine had already slipped away.
After another failed attempt to capture Levine in Guatemala, the FBI heard from Austrian authorities in May 2020.

Austrian authorities informed the FBI in May 2020 that a facial ID system had identified someone who looked like Levine, who was trying to open a bank account in Austria using a Mexican passport, according to the DOJ.
Levine was arrested in June and extradited to the US.
Justice Department officials say Levine had scammed more than 20 people out of hundreds of thousands of dollars.
Levine has also been charged by the US with running a cryptocurrency scam.
A criminal complaint filed against Levine and an alleged accomplice accuses him of stealing $5 million from two victims, after promising that he would give them Bitcoin in return.
According to prosecutors, Levine never sent the promised Bitcoin.

Randy Craig Levine was charged with one count of conspiring to commit commodities fraud, one count of conspiring to commit wire fraud, two counts of commodities fraud, two counts of wire fraud, and one count of money laundering; prosecutors said he "induced others to send millions of dollars" after "falsely representing that he intended to sell large quantities of Bitcoin to buyers."

In the Southern District of Florida case, Levine was described as a 54-year-old Boca Raton resident who "formerly" operated three sports-betting websites from his home in Highland Beach and had "fled the United States" in 2005; the same reporting says he had been on the lam for 15 years and does not identify any prior criminal conviction.

Levine ran www.baseballpicks.net, www.nflfootballpicks.tv, and www.nbabasket-ballpicks.net from 1999 through July 2004, told customers he would open offshore or Las Vegas casino gambling accounts with their money, and then "never opened the promised gambling accounts" but instead used the money for personal gain.
From 1999 through July 2004, Randy Craig Levine operated three internet web sites and defrauded more than 25 victims.
In 2018, Levine and Philip Reichenthal induced two separate groups of investors to send Reichenthal a combined total of over $5.3 million to buy bitcoin from Levine.

On September 14, 2020, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York announced a complaint charging Randy Craig Levine and Philip Reichenthal with commodities fraud, wire fraud, and money laundering offenses in connection with a deceptive cryptocurrency scheme that induced investors to send more than $5 million for bitcoin purchases.
The CFTC reported that Levine was ordered to pay forfeiture commensurate with restitution after his March 21, 2023 sentence.

From on or about April 29, 2019 through on or about May 21, 2019, Randy Craig Levine and Philip Reichenthal allegedly induced victims to send more than $5 million for Bitcoin purchases, while Levine was also charged for a 1999–2004 sports-betting scheme and later pleaded guilty on November 9, 2022.

The complaint says Levine allegedly induced others to send millions of dollars to Reichenthal to fund Bitcoin purchases after falsely claiming he would sell large quantities of Bitcoin, and the CFTC later said the scheme involved over $5 million in restitution.

The closest documented parallel case in the available sources is the related Philip Reichenthal matter, where the CFTC said both men were ordered to pay over $5 million in restitution after pleading guilty in the parallel SDNY criminal case.
The Miami U.S. Attorney’s Office said Levine defrauded more than 25 victims in the sports-betting website scheme.
The CFTC said Levine and Reichenthal had made false representations to investors that induced them to send over $5 million to Reichenthal to buy bitcoin from Levine.
The total fraud alleged exceeds $5 million in cryptocurrency fraud
In the first scheme, Individual-1 wired over $3 million to Reichenthal to fund the purchase of Bitcoin
After receiving the $3 million, Reichenthal wired over $2 million to bank accounts in Guatemala
In the second scheme, investors sent over $2 million to Reichenthal to fund the purchase of Bitcoin
After receiving the funds in the second scheme, Reichenthal sent over $1.9 million to bank accounts in Mexico controlled by Levine

The disciplinary charges against Reichenthal related to his 'receipt of approximately $2,125,000.00 in escrow funds and subsequent failure to disburse in accordance with the escrow agreement' as stated in court documents
The sentencing judge ordered Levine to pay over $600,000 in restitution to his victims.
Levine defrauded more than 25 victims.
Investors were induced to send over $5 million to Reichenthal to buy bitcoin from Levine.
The combined total sent by two separate groups of investors was over $5.3 million.
The total restitution imposed is over $5 million.

After the gambling case, Levine remained a fugitive for nearly 15 years until his June 2020 arrest in Austria using facial-recognition identification, and the later criminal case led to his separate cryptocurrency prosecution and sentencing.

Philip Reichenthal was Levine's central associate in the cryptocurrency case, and prosecutors said Levine sent money to Reichenthal to buy Bitcoin after allegedly misrepresenting that he had Bitcoin to sell.

A 2020 reporting and court-record summary described Randy Craig Levine as a former Coral Springs resident who was 53 years old and a former international fugitive wanted in a cryptocurrency-fraud case.

The record describes Levine’s case as centering on a fake bitcoin-brokerage scheme in which victims were told their money would be used to buy bitcoin, but the alleged conspirators never bought the bitcoin and instead diverted investor funds.
In the criminal complaint, Levine was identified by multiple aliases, including Viktor Lapin, Andre Santiago Santos Galindo, Alexander Martinez Lavrov, Alexander Kozlov, and Hristo Danielov Marinov.
Levine fled the US in 2005, after authorities seized his passport as part of an investigation into an alleged scam he had been running, the DOJ said.

The Southern District of New York press release said Levine and Reichenthal were charged in an "over $5 million cryptocurrency fraud" and alleged that Levine "induced others to send millions of dollars to REICHENTHAL" after "falsely representing" a Bitcoin sale; the release was issued by Acting U.S. Attorney Audrey Strauss and FBI Assistant Director-in-Charge William F. Sweeney Jr.
